questions.q: What is the core idea behind Zero-Noise Extrapolation?
options: Average many runs at exactly the same noise level to cancel out error
Measure the result at several deliberately amplified noise levels, then extrapolate the trend back to the unreachable zero-noise point
Run the circuit with all noise sources physically disabled on the hardware
Only use simulators, which have no noise by default
questions.explain: ZNE deliberately runs the same circuit at multiple artificially amplified noise-scale factors, then fits and extrapolates a curve back to λ=0 — a point you can never run directly on real hardware, but can estimate from the trend.

questions.q: How does gate folding (replacing gate G with G·G⁻¹·G) amplify noise without changing the circuit's intended computation?
options: It deletes the gate entirely, simplifying the circuit
G·G⁻¹·G is mathematically equivalent to G in the ideal case, but each of the three real executions adds real hardware error, roughly tripling accumulated error
It replaces the gate with a completely different, unrelated gate
It only works on measurement operations, not gates
questions.explain: In the noiseless, ideal case G·G⁻¹·G cancels out exactly to G, so the intended computation is unchanged. But on real hardware each of the three gate executions carries its own error, so the effective accumulated error roughly triples.

questions.q: Using the teaching model E(1)=0.72 and E(2)=0.64, what does the linear extrapolation E(0) = 2·E(1) − E(2) give, and what does that number represent?
options: 0.68, the average of the two measurements
0.80, the extrapolated estimate of the ideal, zero-noise expectation value
0.56, the expectation value at triple noise
1.44, the sum of both measurements
questions.explain: 2(0.72) − 0.64 = 0.80, which in this deliberately linear teaching model exactly recovers E_ideal — the hypothetical zero-noise expectation value that was never actually measured directly.

questions.q: Why was the E(λ) = E_ideal + slope·λ relationship in this lesson deliberately built to be exactly linear?
options: So the extrapolation arithmetic is fully checkable by hand, even though real hardware noise scaling is often only approximately linear and can look closer to exponential at larger λ
Because linear models always give more accurate results than exponential ones
Because Qiskit only supports linear noise models
Because all real quantum hardware noise is exactly linear in λ
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that real noise scaling is usually only approximately linear, and this example was constructed to be exactly linear on purpose so the hand arithmetic works out cleanly — not as a claim that real hardware behaves this way.

questions.q: Which real production tools apply ZNE in practice, as named in this lesson?
options: Only `qiskit_aer.noise`, with no other tools involved
`NumPy` and `SciPy` exclusively
The `qiskit.visualization` module
The `mitiq` library (built to work with Qiskit circuits), and the `resilience_level` option on qiskit-ibm-runtime's `EstimatorV2` primitive
questions.explain: mitiq is a dedicated mitigation library that implements ZNE (among other techniques) for Qiskit circuits, and EstimatorV2's resilience_level option can apply ZNE automatically when running on real IBM hardware.
